overview.one_sentence: QWEN introduces a series of open-source large language models (1.8B, 7B, and 14B parameters) with specialized variants for coding and mathematics, achieving competitive performance on benchmarks while enabling tool-use and agent capabilities.
overview.problem: Existing large language models lack reproducibility, steerability, and accessibility, with proprietary models dominating performance benchmarks while open-source alternatives struggle with alignment, scalability, and domain-specific tasks.
overview.solution: QWEN combines extensive pretraining on 3 trillion tokens with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), alongside specialized domain adaptations for coding and mathematics, ensuring open accessibility and strong performance.
overview.why_it_matters: QWEN bridges the gap between proprietary and open-source models by delivering competitive performance on benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) while enabling tool-use, agentic behavior, and domain specialization—all while being openly accessible for further research.

key_specs.label: Pretraining Data
key_specs.value: Up to 3 trillion tokens (text + code, multilingual)

key_specs.label: Tokenization
key_specs.value: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) with 152K vocabulary (cl100k base + Chinese/language-specific tokens)

key_specs.label: Architecture
key_specs.value: Modified Transformer (LLaMA-based) with untied embeddings, RoPE positional embeddings (FP32 inverse frequency), SwiGLU activation, RMSNorm, and bias in QKV layers

key_specs.label: Context Length
key_specs.value: 2048 tokens (pretraining), extendable to 8192+ via NTK-aware interpolation + window attention

contributions.title: Open-Source Scalability with Competitive Performance
contributions.summary: Releases 7B and 14B base/aligned models with strong benchmarks (e.g., QWEN-14B outperforms LLaMA2-70B in 3/7 tasks) while maintaining open accessibility.
contributions.importance: First open-source series to rival proprietary models (e.g., GPT-3.5) on key benchmarks without proprietary data constraints.

contributions.title: NTK-Aware Context Extension
contributions.summary: Dynamic NTK-aware interpolation + window attention enables 8192+ token context without performance degradation, addressing quadratic complexity limitations.
contributions.importance: Preserves model accuracy while extending context length for long-document tasks (e.g., code interpretation, agent planning).

contributions.title: Multilingual Tokenization Efficiency
contributions.summary: 152K-vocabulary BPE tokenizer achieves superior compression (e.g., 30%+ better than XLM-R in 14 languages) while maintaining downstream performance.
contributions.importance: Reduces inference costs without sacrificing accuracy, critical for multilingual and code-heavy applications.

contributions.title: Specialized Domain Adaptation
contributions.summary: CODE-QWEN and MATH-QWEN-CHAT outperform generalist models on coding (HumanEval: +23% pass@1) and math (GSM8K: +10% vs. QWEN-CHAT) benchmarks.
contributions.importance: Demonstrates that domain-specific pretraining (90B code tokens) and fine-tuning can close gaps with proprietary models.

contributions.title: Tool-Use and Agent Benchmarks
contributions.summary: Publicly released benchmarks for ReAct prompting, code interpreter tasks, and Hugging Face Agent framework evaluate QWEN’s agentic capabilities (e.g., 98% tool selection accuracy in 14B model).
contributions.importance: Provides standardized evaluation for LLM-agent research, enabling reproducible comparisons across models.

key_findings.title: Benchmark Performance (Base Models)
key_findings.summary: QWEN-14B outperforms LLaMA2-70B in 3/7 tasks (MMLU: 66.3 vs. 63.7, GSM8K: 61.3 vs. 54.4) and matches proprietary models on math (MATH: 24.8 vs. GPT-3.5’s 34.1).

key_findings.title: Alignment via RLHF
key_findings.summary: QWEN-CHAT-RLHF achieves 70.5% win rate vs. GPT-3.5 in human evaluation (300 Chinese instructions), surpassing SFT models (58.7% win rate) and falling behind GPT-4 (86.7% win rate).

key_findings.title: Coding Specialization
key_findings.summary: CODE-QWEN-CHAT-14B achieves 66.4% pass@1 on HumanEval (vs. GPT-4’s 86.6%) and 51.9% avg. pass@1 on HUMANEVALPACK (vs. WizardCoder’s 40.5%), outperforming generalist models.

key_findings.title: Math Specialization
key_findings.summary: MATH-QWEN-CHAT-14B achieves 69.8% GSM8K accuracy (vs. GPT-3.5’s 80.8%) and 24.2% MATH accuracy (vs. Minerva-62B’s 27.6%), approaching proprietary models with 14B parameters.

limitations.title: Quadratic Memory Complexity
limitations.summary: Self-attention mechanisms require O(N²) memory for sequence length N, limiting practical context lengths without optimizations (e.g., sparse attention).
limitations.details: NTK-aware interpolation mitigates this for inference but does not eliminate memory bottlenecks for extremely long documents (>32K tokens).

limitations.title: RLHF Alignment Tax
limitations.summary: RLHF fine-tuning may reduce generalization to out-of-distribution tasks (e.g., math/coding) compared to SFT, requiring careful tuning of pretrained gradient coefficients.
limitations.details: Empirical findings show alignment tax is mitigated with sufficient pretraining data but remains a challenge for domain-specific tasks.

limitations.title: Benchmark Limitations
limitations.summary: Traditional benchmarks (e.g., MMLU) may not fully capture chat model capabilities (e.g., tool-use, creativity), necessitating human evaluation for comprehensive assessment.
limitations.details: Human evaluation shows QWEN-CHAT-RLHF outperforms SFT models but still lags behind GPT-4 in complex, open-ended tasks.

limitations.title: Proprietary Model Gap
limitations.summary: QWEN falls behind GPT-4 in tool-use (e.g., 98% vs. 100% tool selection accuracy) and agentic reasoning, highlighting areas for future improvement.
limitations.details: Gaps persist in multimodal tasks (e.g., QWEN-VL not evaluated here) and highly specialized domains (e.g., advanced math problem-solving).

nodes.label: Untied Embedding and Output Projection
nodes.description: Separate weight matrices for input embeddings and output projection to improve performance at the cost of increased memory usage, deviating from the tied-weight approach.
nodes.how_it_works: Input embeddings and output projection are computed independently without weight tying, allowing for more expressive power.

nodes.label: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE)
nodes.description: Positional encoding method using rotary embeddings to inject positional information into token embeddings, adopted from prior work (Su et al., 2021).
nodes.how_it_works: Applies rotary transformations to token embeddings to encode positional information, improving long-range dependencies.

nodes.label: Bias in QKV Layer
nodes.description: Biases added to the QKV projections in the attention layer to enhance extrapolation capabilities, contrasting with bias removal in other layers.
nodes.how_it_works: Adds learnable bias terms to the query, key, and value projections in the attention mechanism.
nodes.paper_term: biases in the QKV layer of attention

nodes.label: Pre-Normalization with RMSNorm
nodes.description: Replaces layer normalization with RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Layer Normalization) for improved training stability and efficiency, following Jiang et al. (2023).
nodes.how_it_works: Normalizes layer inputs using RMSNorm before passing them to subsequent layers, improving gradient flow and training dynamics.

nodes.label: SwiGLU Activation
nodes.description: Combined Swish and Gated Linear Unit (GLU) activation function, empirically shown to outperform alternatives like GeLU in initial experiments.
nodes.how_it_works: Applies a gated linear unit mechanism combined with Swish activation to the feed-forward network, enabling selective information flow.

nodes.label: Reduced Feed-Forward Network Dimension
nodes.description: Feed-forward network dimension reduced from 4x hidden size to 8/3x hidden size, deviating from the conventional 4x scaling.
nodes.how_it_works: Limits the intermediate dimension of the feed-forward layer to 8/3 of the hidden size, balancing capacity and efficiency.

equations.title: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE)
equations.explanation: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) applies a rotation matrix to the input embeddings to encode positional information. The rotation matrix is parameterized by an inverse frequency matrix, where each position `i` is assigned a unique rotation angle `θ_i` based on a maximum frequency `θ_max` and model dimension `d_model`. This method avoids the need for explicit positional embeddings and instead encodes positional information in the query and key matrices of the attention mechanism.

variables.name: Rotation Matrix
variables.meaning: A 2x2 rotation matrix applied to embeddings to encode positional information.

variables.name: Rotation Angle for Position `i`
variables.meaning: The rotation angle for the `i`-th position, calculated using the inverse frequency scaling.

variables.name: Maximum Frequency
variables.meaning: A hyperparameter defining the highest frequency in the inverse frequency matrix.

variables.name: Model Dimension
variables.meaning: The dimensionality of the model embeddings.

variables.name: Position Index
variables.meaning: The index of the token in the sequence, ranging from 0 to sequence length.

variables.name: Relative Position Index
variables.meaning: The relative position between two tokens in the attention mechanism.

equations.title: SwiGLU Activation Function
equations.explanation: SwiGLU (Swish-Gated Linear Unit) is a gated activation function that combines the Swish activation with a gating mechanism. It applies a gating mechanism to the input `x` using two learned weight matrices `W_1` and `W_2`, followed by a linear transformation `W_3`. The gating mechanism allows the network to learn which parts of the input should be amplified or suppressed, improving performance over traditional activation functions.

variables.name: Swish Activation
variables.meaning: $\sigma(x) = x \cdot \sigma(x)$ where $\sigma(x)$ is the sigmoid function.

variables.name: Input Vector
variables.meaning: The input to the SwiGLU activation function, typically the output of a linear transformation.

variables.name: Weight Matrix for Swish
variables.meaning: Learned weight matrix applied to the input before applying the Swish activation.

variables.name: Weight Matrix for Gating
variables.meaning: Learned weight matrix applied to the input for the gating mechanism.

variables.name: Output Weight Matrix
variables.meaning: Learned weight matrix applied to the gated output before final linear transformation.

variables.name: Bias Terms
variables.meaning: Bias terms added to the respective linear transformations.

equations.title: Feed-Forward Network (FFN) Dimension Scaling
equations.explanation: The dimension of the feed-forward network (FFN) in the Transformer architecture is scaled down from the traditional 4 times the hidden size to $\frac{8}{3}$ times the hidden size. This adjustment reduces computational cost while maintaining model performance.

variables.name: Feed-Forward Network Dimension
variables.meaning: The dimensionality of the intermediate layer in the FFN.

variables.name: Hidden Size
variables.meaning: The dimensionality of the hidden layer in the Transformer model.

code_snippets.title: qwen_transformer_block.py
code_snippets.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

class QWENBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.config = config
        hidden_size = config.hidden_size
        num_heads = config.num_attention_heads
        head_dim = hidden_size // num_heads

        # Attention
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(
            embed_dim=hidden_size,
            num_heads=num_heads,
            bias=True,  # QKV bias for extrapolation
            dropout=config.attention_dropout
        )

        # RMSNorm
        self.norm1 = nn.RMSNorm(hidden_size, eps=1e-6)
        self.norm2 = nn.RMSNorm(hidden_size, eps=1e-6)

        # Feed-forward
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_size, int(8/3 * hidden_size)),
            SwiGLU(hidden_size),
            nn.Linear(int(8/3 * hidden_size), hidden_size)
        )

    def forward(self, x, rotary_embeddings=None):
        # Self-attention with RoPE
        x_norm = self.norm1(x)
        x_attn, _ = self.attn(
            query=x_norm, key=x_norm, value=x_norm,
            attn_mask=None, need_weights=False
        )
        if rotary_embeddings:
            x_attn = x_attn * rotary_embeddings
        x = x + x_attn

        # Feed-forward with SwiGLU
        x_norm = self.norm2(x)
        x_ffn = self.ffn(x_norm)
        x = x + x_ffn
        return x

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear1 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, 2 * hidden_size)
        self.linear2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.linear1(x)
        x1, x2 = x.chunk(2, dim=-1)
        return x2 * F.silu(x1) * self.linear2(x2)

metadata.title: QWEN: A Pioneer Large Language Model Series
metadata.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of artificial intelligence, enabling natural language processing tasks that were previously thought to be exclusive to humans. In this work, we introduce QWEN1, the first installment of our large language model series. QWEN is a comprehensive language model series that encompasses distinct models with varying parameter counts. It includes QWEN, the base pretrained language models, and QWEN-CHAT, the chat models finetuned with human alignment techniques. The base language models consistently demonstrate superior performance across a multitude of downstream tasks, and the chat models, particularly those trained using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), are highly competitive. The chat models possess advanced tool-use and planning capabilities for creating agent applications, showcasing impressive performance even when compared to bigger models on complex tasks like utilizing a code interpreter. Furthermore, we have developed coding-specialized models, CODE-QWEN and CODE-QWEN-CHAT, as well as mathematics-focused models, MATH-QWEN-CHAT, which are built upon base language models. These models demonstrate significantly improved performance in comparison with open-source models, and slightly fall behind the proprietary models.
